also_built_by: Hindustan Aeronautics, Aero Vodochody, Chengdu Aircraft Industry
description:
The MiG-21 is a single-seat, single-engine supersonic fighter and interceptor designed by the Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau in the early 1950s. It met a Soviet requirement for a small, cheap day fighter able to reach Mach 2, using a tailed delta wing and a nose intake with a movable shock cone to regulate airflow.

It entered service in 1959 and became the most-produced supersonic aircraft, with 11,496 built in the Soviet Union, India and Czechoslovakia, plus further Chinese Chengdu J-7 derivatives. More than fifty air forces operated it. It fought over Vietnam, in the Arab-Israeli wars of 1967 and 1973, and in the Indo-Pakistani conflicts of 1971 and 1999.

The circular nose intake, the cropped delta wing spanning only 7.15 metres, and the narrow fuselage built around the engine are the type's clearest recognition features.

The UH-1 is a single-engine utility helicopter developed by Bell to meet a 1955 US Army requirement for a turbine-powered medical evacuation and general-purpose aircraft. The prototype XH-40 first flew in 1956. The original designation HU-1 produced the name Huey, which outlasted the official name Iroquois.

The type entered service in 1959 and defined helicopter air mobility in Vietnam, where it flew troop assault, medical evacuation, resupply and gunship missions. More than 16,000 were built, with licence production in Italy, Japan, Germany and Taiwan, and service with dozens of armed forces and civil operators. The US Army retired the UH-1H in 2005; derivatives such as the UH-1Y remain in service.

The two-bladed main rotor, which produces the characteristic slapping beat, the skid landing gear and the wide sliding cabin doors distinguish it.

The T-33 is a two-seat jet trainer developed by Lockheed from the P-80 Shooting Star fighter. The fuselage was lengthened by about a metre to fit a second cockpit and instructor position, producing the first jet trainer to be built in large numbers. It first flew in 1948.

Lockheed built 6,557, with a further 656 assembled by Canadair as the CT-133 Silver Star and 210 by Kawasaki in Japan. Beyond advanced pilot training it served as a proficiency, target-towing, reconnaissance and light attack aircraft, and armed versions were exported widely. More than thirty air forces flew the type; the last military examples were withdrawn in 2017.

The permanently fitted wingtip fuel tanks, the long tandem canopy and the straight, thin wing inherited from the P-80 identify it.

also_built_by: Canadair, Fiat, Aeritalia, Messerschmitt, Fokker, SABCA, Mitsubishi
description:
The F-104 is a single-seat, single-engine supersonic interceptor designed at Lockheed under Kelly Johnson after discussions with fighter pilots returning from Korea, who wanted speed and rate of climb above all else. The result was a minimal airframe with a very short, thin trapezoidal wing and a J79 turbojet. It first flew in 1954 and entered service in 1958.

USAF use was brief, but the multi-role F-104G was adopted across NATO and produced by European consortia in Germany, Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands, as well as in Canada and Japan. Of 2,578 built, most came from these licence lines. The German fleet suffered a high accident rate. Italy retired the last examples in 2004.

The 6.63-metre wing, with leading edges sharp enough to require protective covers on the ground, and the T-tail are its distinguishing features.
engines: 1 x General Electric J79 afterburning turbojet

also_built_by: Canadair, Mitsubishi, Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation, Fiat
description:
The F-86 is a single-seat transonic day fighter built by North American Aviation. A straight-wing design was revised around captured German swept-wing research, giving 35 degrees of sweep and a substantial speed gain. It first flew in October 1947 and entered service in 1949 as the first swept-wing fighter in the United States Air Force.

It is best known for air combat over Korea against the MiG-15, and later served in the Taiwan Strait and the 1965 and 1971 Indo-Pakistani wars. Production reached 9,860, including 1,815 by Canadair, 300 by Mitsubishi, 221 by Fiat and 112 Avon-engined aircraft by Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation in Australia. Around thirty air forces operated the type, the last into the 1990s.

The oval nose intake, swept wing and low bubble canopy are its recognition points.

The F-4 Phantom II is a twin-engine, two-seat supersonic fighter designed by McDonnell Aircraft in the mid-1950s as a carrier-based fleet defence interceptor for the US Navy, armed only with radar-guided missiles and carrying no internal gun. It first flew on 27 May 1958.

Its performance led the US Air Force and Marine Corps to adopt it as a multirole fighter and fighter-bomber. Phantoms flew air-to-air, strike and Wild Weasel missions throughout the Vietnam War, and served with eleven other air arms including Israel, Iran, West Germany, Britain, Japan, Greece, Turkey and South Korea. Production ran from 1958 to 1981 and totalled 5,195, of which 138 were assembled under licence by Mitsubishi.

The type is recognised by the 12-degree dihedral of its outer wing panels and the 23-degree anhedral tailplane, both adopted to correct stability problems found during early flight testing.
engines: 2 x General Electric J79-GE-17A afterburning turbojets

description:
The C-47 Skytrain is a twin-engine military transport developed by Douglas Aircraft from the DC-3 airliner, fitted with a reinforced cabin floor, a large two-part cargo door and provision for paratroops, glider towing and casualty evacuation. The first C-47 flew on 23 December 1941.

It carried airborne troops on D-Day, at Arnhem and across the Rhine, flew the Hump route from India to China, and formed the backbone of the 1948-49 Berlin Airlift. Douglas built 10,174 military examples. The Soviet Union produced the design under licence as the Lisunov Li-2 and Japan as the Showa and Nakajima L2D. British and Commonwealth crews knew it as the Dakota.

Military airframes are distinguished from civil DC-3s by the wide cargo door on the port side, the navigator's astrodome above the cockpit, and the glider tow attachment under the tail.
engines: 2 x Pratt & Whitney R-1830-90C Twin Wasp radials

description:
The AH-1 Cobra is a two-seat attack helicopter developed by Bell Helicopter as a private venture in 1965, mating the engine, transmission and rotor system of the UH-1 Iroquois to a new slim fuselage with the gunner seated ahead of and below the pilot. It answered an urgent US Army requirement for an armed escort in Vietnam, and the Model 209 prototype flew on 7 September 1965.

The AH-1G entered service in 1967. Single-engine AH-1S and AH-1F models served the US Army until 2001, while the twin-engine AH-1J, AH-1T and AH-1W SuperCobra and the four-blade AH-1Z Viper equipped the US Marine Corps. About 2,390 of all versions were built, with exports to Israel, Japan, Turkey, Jordan, Iran, Pakistan and South Korea.

The fuselage is barely a metre wide, with stub wings for rockets and a chin turret under the nose.

The MiG-23 is a single-seat, single-engine variable-geometry fighter designed by the Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau to replace the MiG-21, correcting that aircraft's short range, light armament, small radar and dependence on long runways. The swing wing gave short-field performance without sacrificing speed. The prototype flew on 10 June 1967.

Entering service in 1970, it became the standard Soviet tactical fighter of the 1970s and 1980s, and the ground-attack MiG-27 was developed from it. It saw combat in the Arab-Israeli wars, Angola, the Iran-Iraq War, Afghanistan and Libya. 5,047 were built between 1967 and 1985 and exported to more than 20 countries.

Visible identifying features are the three wing sweep positions, the box-section side air intakes, and the large ventral fin that folds sideways for landing clearance.

The Mi-8 is a twin-turbine medium transport helicopter designed by the Mil bureau from 1960 to replace the piston-engined Mi-4, with two turboshafts mounted above a cabin seating 24 troops or carrying four tonnes of freight. The single-engine V-8 prototype flew on 7 July 1961; the definitive twin-engine configuration followed in 1962.

It entered Soviet service in 1967 and has been produced at Kazan and Ulan-Ude ever since, in transport, armed assault, airborne command post, minelaying and electronic warfare forms. More than 17,000 have been built, making it the most-produced helicopter in history, and it has served with over 80 air arms. The uprated TV3-117 versions are marketed for export as the Mi-17.

Characteristic features are the clamshell rear loading doors, the five-blade main rotor, and the tail rotor mounted on the starboard side on early production aircraft.

The MiG-17 is a single-seat transonic jet fighter developed by the Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau from 1949 as a redesign of the MiG-15, to correct that aircraft's poor handling near its speed limit. The main changes were a thinner compound-sweep wing, 45 degrees inboard and 42 outboard, and a lengthened fuselage. It first flew on 14 January 1950 and entered service in October 1952.

Production totalled 10,649 including the Polish Lim-5 and Lim-6, the Czechoslovak S-104 and the Chinese Shenyang J-5. It was exported to more than 40 air forces and saw combat in the Taiwan Strait, the Middle East and Vietnam, where North Vietnamese pilots used its turn rate and cannon armament against the faster F-105 and F-4.

It is distinguished from the MiG-15 by a longer fuselage, three wing fences per wing and a ventral fin. Armament sits under the nose intake: one 37 mm and two 23 mm cannon.

The An-2 is a single-engine biplane utility transport designed by Oleg Antonov's bureau and first flown on 31 August 1947. It was built to replace the Polikarpov Po-2 in agriculture, forestry and short-field transport across Soviet territory where prepared runways did not exist. Fabric-covered wings with full-span leading-edge slats and slotted flaps give it a stall speed of roughly 50 km/h and take-off runs of a few hundred metres.

Production ran from 1947 to 2001 and exceeded 18,000 aircraft, more than 13,000 of them built by WSK PZL-Mielec in Poland and further batches in China as the Y-5. Operators ranged from Aeroflot feeder services and crop-spraying fleets to Warsaw Pact military transport and parachute training units.

It is the largest single-engine biplane to have entered mass production, powered by a 1,010 hp Shvetsov ASh-62IR nine-cylinder radial.

The F-84 is a single-seat Republic Aviation fighter-bomber built in two distinct forms. The straight-wing Thunderjet first flew on 28 February 1946 and entered service in November 1947 as an escort fighter that proved better suited to ground attack. The swept-wing F-84F Thunderstreak, flown in 1950 and in service from 1954, was a substantially new aircraft with a Wright J65 engine.

In Korea the Thunderjet became the primary USAF strike type, flying 86,408 sorties. The F-84G was the first fighter cleared to carry a nuclear weapon. Production reached 7,524 straight-wing aircraft and 3,428 F-84F and RF-84F, 1,301 of the latter going to NATO air forces under mutual defence aid. The USAF retired the type in 1964; Greek F-84Fs flew until 1991.

Straight-wing aircraft carry permanent wingtip fuel tanks; the F-84F is recognised by its swept surfaces and taller fin; the RF-84F Thunderflash moved its intakes to the wing roots.

The Mi-2 is a light turbine helicopter designed by the Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant in the early 1960s as a successor to the piston-engined Mi-1. Two small turboshafts mounted above the cabin replaced the single radial, roughly doubling useful load while carrying a pilot and eight passengers or 700 kg of internal cargo.

The prototype flew in the Soviet Union on 22 September 1961, after which development and all production were transferred to Poland in 1964, making it the only Soviet-designed helicopter built entirely outside the USSR. WSK PZL-Swidnik completed 5,497 by 1998, about a third for military users; the remainder went to agricultural spraying, air ambulance, training and passenger work with Aeroflot and Eastern Bloc operators.

It is identified by the pair of slender engine nacelles sitting above and ahead of the cabin roof and a three-blade main rotor of 14.5 m diameter.

The MiG-15 is a single-seat swept-wing jet fighter developed by Mikoyan-Gurevich, first flown on 30 December 1947 and in service from 1949. It was built around the Rolls-Royce Nene centrifugal turbojet, sold to the USSR in 1946 and produced as the Klimov RD-45, and its 35-degree wing sweep drew on German wartime aerodynamic research. The armament of one 37 mm and two 23 mm cannon was chosen for attacking bombers.

Over Korea from 1950 it outclassed the straight-wing UN jets and forced the rapid deployment of the F-86 Sabre. Some 13,130 were built in the Soviet Union and at least 4,180 more under licence as the Polish Lim-1 and Lim-2 and the Czechoslovak S-102 and S-103, equipping some 40 air forces.

Recognition points include two wing fences per wing, the nose intake split around the cockpit and rear-fuselage airbrakes. Many surviving examples are two-seat UTI MiG-15 trainers.

also_built_by: Canadair, CASA, F+W Emmen, Korean Air, AIDC
description:
The F-5 is a light supersonic fighter developed by Northrop from the mid-1950s around a pair of small General Electric J85 turbojets, sharing much of its structure with the T-38 Talon trainer. It was designed to be cheap to buy and simple to maintain, and the initial F-5A/B Freedom Fighter was built largely for supply to allied air forces under US military assistance programmes rather than for the USAF itself.

The improved F-5E/F Tiger II, with more thrust, greater wing area and a fire-control radar, won the 1970 International Fighter Aircraft competition. Roughly 2,600 were built, with additional licence production in Canada, Spain, Switzerland, South Korea and Taiwan. More than thirty air forces flew the type, and the US Navy and Air Force used it as a dissimilar air combat aggressor.

Its small size is the obvious feature: under 15 m long, with a sharp nose, sharply swept wing-root extensions and two closely spaced exhaust nozzles.
engines: 2 x General Electric J85-GE-21 afterburning turbojets

description:
The Hunter is a single-seat transonic jet fighter designed by Hawker under Sydney Camm to replace the Gloster Meteor as the RAF's day interceptor. It first flew on 20 July 1951 and entered service in 1954, combining a swept wing with a Rolls-Royce Avon turbojet and a removable pack of four 30 mm ADEN cannon.

After the supersonic English Electric Lightning took over interception duties in the early 1960s, the Hunter was reworked as a fighter-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. A total of 1,972 were built, including licence production by Fokker in the Netherlands and Avions Fairey and SABCA in Belgium, and the type was exported to 21 overseas air forces. It saw combat with India and Pakistan, in the Middle East and over Aden; Lebanon flew Hunters until 2014.

The cannon pack under the nose and the single ventral airbrake are distinguishing features.

The A-4 Skyhawk is a single-seat, subsonic, carrier-capable light attack aircraft designed by Ed Heinemann at Douglas for the US Navy. The requirement was for a jet able to deliver a nuclear weapon from a carrier deck, and Heinemann's answer came in at roughly half the weight the Navy had specified. The delta wing was small enough to need no folding mechanism, saving weight and complexity.

It first flew on 22 June 1954 and entered service in 1956. Production ran until 1979 and totalled 2,960 aircraft. The Skyhawk flew large numbers of strike sorties over Vietnam with the US Navy and Marine Corps, served with Israel from 1967 onwards, and was used by Argentina against British ships in the 1982 Falklands conflict.

The short span, the tall tricycle undercarriage and the dorsal avionics hump on later aircraft are recognisable features.

The Mirage III is a single-seat delta-wing supersonic fighter developed by Dassault in France in response to a 1952 requirement for a lightweight all-weather interceptor able to climb quickly to high altitude. The prototype flew on 17 November 1956 and the type entered service in 1961. The tailless delta layout gave a large wing area, high internal fuel volume and Mach 2 capability on a single SNECMA Atar turbojet.

A total of 1,422 were built, with licence assembly in Australia and Switzerland, and the design spawned the Mirage 5, Mirage 50 and Israeli and South African derivatives. Israel's Mirage IIICs dominated the air fighting of the 1967 Six-Day War, and the type also fought in the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war, the South African Border War and the 1982 Falklands conflict.

The unbroken delta wing with no tailplane is the clearest identifying feature.

The Spitfire is a British single-seat fighter designed by R. J. Mitchell at Supermarine to a 1934 Air Ministry specification for a high-performance monoplane interceptor. It used an all-metal stressed-skin structure, a thin elliptical wing chosen to house the guns and undercarriage while keeping drag low, and a Rolls-Royce Merlin V-12. The prototype flew on 5 March 1936 and the type entered RAF service in August 1938.

More than 20,351 were built in 24 marks, the largest share at the Castle Bromwich shadow factory. Spitfires flew alongside the Hurricane in the Battle of Britain and served in every RAF theatre as interceptor, photo-reconnaissance aircraft and fighter-bomber, with later marks using the larger Griffon engine. The last RAF operational sortie was flown on 1 April 1954.

The elliptical wing planform and the narrow-track undercarriage remain the type's most recognisable features.

The Aero L-29 Delfin is a two-seat jet basic trainer designed in Czechoslovakia in the late 1950s. It was built to give Warsaw Pact air forces a single, simple type for the whole early jet training sequence, replacing piston trainers and a patchwork of national designs. The layout is deliberately conservative: straight mid-mounted wing, T-tail, and one low-thrust Motorlet M-701 turbojet fed by side intakes.

In 1961 the design won a Warsaw Pact comparative trial against the Polish TS-11 and Soviet Yak-30, and it became the standard trainer across most of the bloc. Production ran from 1963 to 1974 and reached 3,665 aircraft, the great majority delivered to the Soviet Union. Exports extended to Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Nigeria, Uganda and Indonesia, and some armed examples flew ground-attack sorties in African and Middle Eastern conflicts.

The rugged airframe and low landing speed that suited rough-field training also made the type cheap to keep flying, and large numbers were sold to private owners after 1990, making the L-29 one of the most common jet warbirds in civil hands.

The Mil Mi-24 is a Soviet attack helicopter that also carries up to eight troops, a combination no Western design adopted. Developed from Mi-8 dynamic components and first flown on 19 September 1969, it was conceived as a flying infantry fighting vehicle: armoured, heavily armed, and able to deliver a squad onto the objective it had just suppressed. Stub wings carry weapon pylons and offload the rotor in fast cruise.

It entered Soviet service in 1972 and became the principal Soviet gunship of the Soviet-Afghan War. Export versions designated Mi-25 and Mi-35 were widely sold, and the type saw combat in the Iran-Iraq War, Angola, Sri Lanka, Chad, Sierra Leone and Ukraine. Roughly 2,648 have been built.

Early variants are recognisable by the wide greenhouse canopy over the tandem crew; from the Mi-24D onward the nose was rebuilt with stepped, heavily framed bubble canopies and a chin turret.

The A-7 Corsair II is an American carrier-capable subsonic light attack aircraft, developed by Ling-Temco-Vought to meet the US Navy's 1963 VAL requirement for a Douglas A-4 Skyhawk replacement. The airframe was derived from the supersonic F-8 Crusader but shortened and made subsonic, trading speed for a large bomb load, long range and a cheaper structure. It was among the first combat aircraft with a head-up display and an inertial navigation and weapons-delivery computer.

First flown on 26 September 1965 and in Navy service by 1 February 1967, it was deployed to Vietnam within the year. The Air Force and Air National Guard adopted the A-7D to replace the A-1 and F-100. American A-7s flew in Grenada, the 1986 Libya raid and the Gulf War. Of 1,545 built, exports went to Greece and Portugal; the Hellenic Air Force retired the last examples in 2014.

The short nose with its large oval chin intake beneath the cockpit is the type's most obvious identifying feature.

also_built_by: Government Aircraft Factories, Glenn L. Martin Company
description:
The English Electric Canberra is a British first-generation jet medium bomber, designed by a team under W. E. W. Petter against a 1944 Air Ministry requirement for a successor to the de Havilland Mosquito. The specification demanded high speed and extreme altitude rather than defensive armament, and the answer was an unswept, very large, low-loading wing on a compact fuselage with two Rolls-Royce Avon turbojets buried in the wings.

It first flew on 13 May 1949 and entered RAF service in May 1951 as the service's first jet bomber. For most of the 1950s it could out-climb any interceptor; in 1957 a Canberra set an altitude record of 70,310 ft. It served in the Suez Crisis, Vietnam, the Indo-Pakistani wars, the Falklands and numerous African conflicts. Some 900 were built in the UK and 49 in Australia by GAF, with licence production in the United States as the Martin B-57. The RAF retired its last in June 2006.

The near-equal span and length, both just under 20 m, and the wide unswept wing distinguish it from later jet bombers.
engines: 2 x Rolls-Royce Avon RA.7 Mk.109 turbojets

description:
The F-100 Super Sabre is an American supersonic fighter and fighter-bomber, the first of the USAF Century Series and the first USAF fighter able to exceed the speed of sound in level flight. North American proposed it in January 1951 as a higher-performance development of the F-86 Sabre, initially called the Sabre 45 for its 45-degree wing sweep. It first flew on 25 May 1953 and entered service on 27 September 1954.

Early service was troubled by yaw instability and inertia coupling, and the fleet was grounded after six major accidents in 1954. The F-100C and F-100D recast the type as a fighter-bomber, and the F-100D became the USAF's primary close air support aircraft over South Vietnam, where 242 F-100s of all models were lost. A total of 2,294 were built; exports went to France, Turkey, Denmark and Taiwan. The Air National Guard retired its last in 1979.

The oval nose intake, thin highly swept wing and one-piece slab tailplane set low on the fuselage are the recognition features.
engines: 1 x Pratt & Whitney J57-P-21A afterburning turbojet
